item.title: APOD: 2026 November 6 – A Farewell to Swift
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:It is time to say goodbye toNASA'sNeil Gehrels Swift Observatory. After nearly 22 years of service, the satellitere-entered Earth's atmosphereon November 4 at 7:39 EST over theNorth Sumatraregion ofIndonesia. Thefeatured imageis a mosaic created in 2018 using some of the first millionimagescaptured by the satellite'sUltraviolet/Optical Telescope. Swift had a combination of instruments, including anX-ray telescopeand agamma-ray telescope, that worked together to enable humanity to study, in unprecedented detail, the fastest and most energeticexplosionsin the universe. The most recentsolar maximumaccelerated the decay of the satellite's orbit. Aninnovative missiontorescue Swiftby boosting its orbit wasnot successful. Swift burned onreentrylike a shooting star, but the impressive data acquired by the telescope over its mission will continue to bring light to the mysteries of the cosmos for years to come. May it keep inspiring new missionsto boldly gointo space, explore new data and seek out new science.Tomorrow's picture:Moon Massif

item.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
item.description:
The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape.
Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today's Mississippi River. In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment. Unencumbered by rugged terrain, the river was free to take a long,meandering pathon itsgradual journeydownslope.
But this part of the San Juan changed when geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward. Some experts think that within the later stages of this “still-enigmatic” history, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s riseelevated the San Juan’s headwaters, which increased the river’sgradientand sped its flow. With that, the water’s erosive power intensified, and the river started carving its winding path deeper and deeper through 300-million-year-old rock.
Today, on its westward path to Lake Powell, the San Juan River flows through an impressive series of entrenched meanders, also known as “goosenecks.” An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the stark desert topography on October 6, 2026.
In Utah’sGoosenecks State Park, the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. In places, it nearly loops back on itself, making horseshoe-shaped bends. One section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 kilometers) apart as the crow—nay, goose—flies.
While the goosenecks are an unusual geologic wonder to behold by day, the area’s dark skies are a spectacle by night. Goosenecks State Park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it anInternational Dark Sky Parkdesignation in 2021. According to DarkSky International, features such as theDouble Cluster in Perseusand theMessier 24 star cloudin the Sagittarius spiral arm of the Milky Way are visible to the unaided eye from the park. InNovember 2026, dark skies offer the chance to view several meteor showers, with the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids, and Leonids reaching their peaks throughout the month.
Astronaut photographISS075-E-188830was acquired on October 6, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of theExpedition 75crew. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. TheInternational Space Station Programsupports the laboratory as part of theISS National Labto help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSCGateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth. Photo byBob Wick (BLM), via Flickr. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: Midwestern City Lights
item.description: City lights from the Midwestern United States to the East Coast sparkle across the landscape a couple of hours before sunrise on Oct. 18, 2026. Major urban areas visible in the photograph include Chicago, Illinois; Detroit, Michigan; and the New York metropolitan region. The International Space Station was orbiting 259 miles above Earth when this photograph was taken.

item.title: NASA Astronauts to Answer Questions from Florida Students
item.description:
Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard theInternational Space Station.
The Earth-to-space call will begin at 10:40 a.m. EST Tuesday, Nov. 10, and will stream live on the agency’s Learn With NASAYouTubechannel.
This event is hosted by Freedom Crossing Academy in St. Johns, Florida, for students in grades K-12, and the community. This unique opportunity aims to deepen understanding of space exploration and enhance awareness of STEM careers.
Media interested in covering the event must RSVP no later than 5 p.m. EST, Monday, Nov. 9, to Christina Upchurch at (904) 547-7517, or atchristina.upchurch@stjohns.k12.fl.us.
For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and to Mars.

item.title: Hubble Learns Galactic History From Stars
item.description:
This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is namedMessier 30(M30) after the French astronomer,Charles Messier, who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus.
M30 is aglobular cluster: a roughly spherical grouping of stars containing anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars. These clusters generally reside on the outskirts of galaxies, orbiting within a vast, diffuse region called the halo like a swarm of moths around a lightbulb. Our Milky Way galaxy has at least 150 globular clusters, the nearest of which is about 6,000 light-years away. These clusters are impressively ancient: astronomers estimate their ages are between 11.5 to 13.5 billion years, making certain globular clusters nearly as old as the universe itself.
Globular clusters have long played an important role in helping us learn about our galaxy. More than a century ago, astronomer Harlow Shapley used observations of a particular type of variable star to measure the locations of and distances to dozens of globular clusters within our galaxy. His work showed that the Sun is not in the center of our galaxy, and that the galactic center lies toward the constellation Sagittarius. (His distance measurements were incorrect, however, and he concluded that our galaxy is about twice as large as it really is.)
Today, astronomers continue to learn about our galaxy by observing globular clusters. Because globular clusters are so ancient, they can give us clues about how our galaxy developed long ago. Globular clusters that formed within our galaxy can act as time capsules, preserving the original chemistry of our young galaxy.
However, it’s possible that not all globular clusters that orbit within our galaxy today formed there. Researchers have discovered that M30 and many other globular clusters orbit in the direction opposite from the way our galaxy spins. This may mean that these clusters did not form within our galaxy at all. Instead, our Milky Way galaxy may have captured them in the distant past!
Hubble has observed M30 multiple times. Apreviously released image of M30featured data from Hubble’sAdvanced Camera for Surveys(ACS) and was part of an observing program (#10775; PI: Sarajedini) that surveyed dozens of Milky Way globular clusters in red and near-infrared light, revealing stars down to just 20% of the mass of the Sun. A more recent program (#13297; PI: Piotto) returned to M30 and other globular clusters in our galaxy, this time observing the clusters with Hubble’sWide Field Camera 3and using three filters that captured bluer light. This program collected data that was critical for studying exotic objects like “blue straggler” stars as well as for investigating the multiple populations of stars that can inhabit a single globular cluster.
More recently, Hubble’s ACS viewed many of these globular clusters again. Those observations were part of a program (#16298, PI: Libralato) that looked at how different populations of stars in globular clusters moved over the 15 years since Hubble first observed them — a feat made possible by Hubble’s longevity and ability to discern fantastically small details in distant objects.
The image above was created with data from all three observing programs and includes the wide range of wavelengths Hubble can see — ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light. Each wavelength helps us better understand how these groups of stars formed and evolved.
Claire AndreoliNASA'sGoddard Space Flight Center,Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov
Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.
These jewels of the night sky offer us a glimpse at the lifecycle of stars.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 5 – Enceladus in Silhouette
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:One of our Solar System's mosttantalizingworlds, Enceladus is backlit by the Sun in this Cassini spacecraft image from November 1, 2009.The dramatic illuminationreveals the plumes that continuously spew into space from the south pole ofSaturn's 500 kilometer diameter moon. Discovered by Cassini in 2005, the icy plumes are likely connected to an oceanbeneath the ice shellof Enceladus. They supply material directly to Saturn's outer, tenuousE ringand make the surface of Enceladus as reflective as snow. Across the scene, Saturn's icy rings scatter sunlight toward Cassini's cameras. Beyond the rings (lower right), the night side of 80 kilometer diameter moonPandorais faintly lit bySaturnlight.Tomorrow's picture:pixels in space

item.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
item.description:
The third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea exposes an ancient piece of the ocean floor and hosts a clowder of cats.
The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during theLate Cretaceous, with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building newoceanic crust. Over time, portions of this oceanic rock were wrenched upward bytectonic forces, eventually emerging as a rugged island made ofophiolite, a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake. Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of theTroodos Mountains.
During theMiocene, considerably younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl, and other marinesedimentary rocksaccumulated around the island, providing material that developed into a second, smaller island to the south during a later period ofgeologic uplift. Over time, sediment poured from rivers into the channel separating the two islands and combined with marine sediments to create deltas and eventually two land bridges, ortombolos. The joined landmass comprises theAkrotiri Peninsula, now the southernmost tip of Cyprus.
The sandy edges of the peninsula were visible whenLandsat 8captured these images on October 10, 2026.Akrotiri Salt Lake, a coastal lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos. The more westerly feature, the Kouris River tombolo, formed first, developing about 50,000 years ago from river-deposited gravels and sands. The eastern tombolo extended southward from Cyprus, cutting off the Mediterranean Sea only within the past 2,000 years,according to geologists.
The lake's water levels now vary markedly with the seasons, typically filling in the late autumn and winter and drying out in the summer. The influx of winter water has historically attracted sizable overwintering flamingo populations, averaging about 4,000 birds. However, the wintering flamingo population has declined in recent years, plummeting to 30 birds in 2025, according tonews reports. Flamingos have long flocked to the lake to feed onfairy shrimp, which are rich in colorful substances called carotenoids that give the birds theirfamously pink hue.
Snakes are another of the island's more notorious animal inhabitants. In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa, or "land of snakes,"likely due to its robust population ofblunt-nosed vipers.According to legend, the island's snake communities grew to be so problematic during a drought in the fourth century that the Roman EmpressHelena, mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control the venomous reptiles.
The first feline imports were released in a particularly snake-infested area on the southeastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata (Cape Cat in Greek). The cape today is still home to theHoly Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats, a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes. Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more thanone millionof the feline predators stalking the island. The handful of nuns who now live in the monastery still care for hundreds of cats, according to theSt. Nicholas Center.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from theU.S. Geological Survey.Story by Adam Voiland.

item.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
item.description:
On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.
The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.
“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”
The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.
“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”
The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight.
With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.
